methodology: The study evaluated printability through fluidity tests, filament extrusion tests, and slump tests using different fiber types (copper-coated steel, polypropylene, basalt) incorporated into concrete mixtures under controlled conditions of superplasticizer content, accelerator content, and silica fume replacement level.
research_objective: Investigate the fundamental workability of 3D printed fiber-reinforced concretes incorporating different fiber types, focusing on fluidity, extrudability, and buildability.

key_findings.finding: Copper-coated steel fibers lead to deteriorated workability, manifested as reduced fluidity, increased fluidity loss over time, poor pumpability, discontinuous extrusion, and low slump.
Polypropylene fibers increase the air content in concrete, thereby improving workability; they exhibit good extrusion continuity, appropriate slump and filament width, and favorable buildability.
Basalt fibers significantly enhance air content and workability; however, due to the high stiffness of the fibers, extrusion continuity is only moderate.
The study aims to analyze the effects of admixture content and fiber type on the fresh workability (particularly printability) of 3D printed concrete materials.

The mix proportions were designed using the controlled variable method with four investigated factors including superplasticizer dosage, accelerator dosage, silica fume replacement rate, and fiber types.

Mixes P1 to P4 were used to investigate the effect of superplasticizer dosage on workability; Mixes P1 and P5 to P7 were used to examine the influence of accelerator dosage; Mixes P1 and P8 to P10 were formulated to assess the impact of silica fume replacement rate; and Mixes P1, P11, and P12 were employed to evaluate the effect of fiber type.
